answer.evidence: The weights that look trained (strong and spatially coherent) form two groups, and both are explained by nodule and lung anatomy. (1) Centre detectors. Units 8, 20, 29, 18, 1 and 2 have broad positive blobs over the central rows (about 5–20) and columns (about 5–18), with weights up to 90–99. Tracing unit 8 through layers 2 and 3 (ignoring ReLU gating) gives a clearly positive net effect on the logit (about +9.6k in integer units, through layer-2 units u3, u6, u7, u10 and u15). So a bright, large central mass pushes toward malignant. (2) Surround detectors. Units 17 and 23 are strongly negative in the centre (unit 17 down to about -97 in rows 8-17, columns 8-16) and positive on the periphery (top rows, bottom rows, right or left edges). Unit 27 is broadly positive over the whole image. These encode the size and extent of the nodule relative to its surroundings and the brightness of nearby structures such as vessels and chest wall. Unit 17's net path is mildly negative (about -2.4k) and unit 23's is negative (about -6k). Neither is a compact patch. No unit shows a small, sharply bounded block of extreme weights in a corner or at an edge, separate from the nodule-centred structure, as an artificial marker would. The densest off-centre cluster (unit 9, rows 15-17, columns 19-22, values about 50-70) is weak, within the range of the random-looking weights, and accompanied by other centre-ish positive spots. It does not justify a shortcut claim.
answer.main_feature: The model mainly measures how much bright, dense tissue sits in the centre of the crop (nodule size and density, extending outward). Larger and brighter central masses push toward malignant, while centre-versus-surround contrast units modulate the score toward benign.
